title: What shapes are left when the corners are cut at the thirds?
description: The corners of an equilateral triangle and of a square, each with sides of nine centimetres, are cut off as far as the marks at the thirds. The video finds the side lengths of the hexagon and the octagon that are left. Keeko's doubt is that the octagon has every side three centimetres.
teaching_notes: One idea: the cut edge of a triangle matches the kept third, but the cut edge of a square is the long side of a right angled triangle and is longer. Watch for students who think the octagon is regular like the hexagon.

source: Cut the corners at the thirds of an equilateral triangle of
video_script.why: The child imagines cutting the corners as the book asks and uses the theorem of Ziva to measure the cut edge of the square.
video_script.substitution: Find the kept third, find the cut edge of one corner, then compare all the sides of the shape left.
video_script.anchor: an imagined equilateral triangle and an imagined square, each with sides of nine centimetres, with their corners cut off at the thirds
video_script.wrong_answer: the octagon has every side three centimetres
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks the octagon is regular like the hexagon, with every side three centimetres. The cut edge of the square is the long side of a right angled corner, so it is longer than three centimetres.
video_script.payoff_line: The triangle leaves a regular hexagon, and the square leaves an octagon that is not regular

final_answer.value: A regular hexagon of side 3 cm; an octagon with sides 3 cm and about 4.24 cm, not regular
final_answer.spoken: a regular hexagon of side three centimetres, and an octagon with sides of three and about four point two four centimetres, not regular

names.Ziva: the theorem used for the shortest path of 40 cm

hold_back: Answer: A regular hexagon of side 3 cm; an octagon with sides 3 cm and about 4.24 cm, not regular
never_show: an octagon with all sides 3 cm marked as right
maths_rules: each side of 9 cm keeps its middle third: 9 / 3 = 3 cm
triangle: each cut corner has a 60 degree angle and two sides of 3 cm, so it is equilateral and the cut edge is 3 cm
the triangle leaves a regular hexagon of side 3 cm
square: each cut corner is a right angled triangle with short sides 3 cm and 3 cm
cut edge: 3 squared = 9, 9 + 9 = 18, so the cut edge is the square root of 18, about 4.24 cm
the octagon has four sides of 3 cm and four sides of about 4.24 cm, so it is not regular
video_script.design: The triangle and the square sit side by side on the stage; the corners are cut off one shape at a time and the sides of the shape left are labelled.

narration: <bookmark mark='third'/>Step one, cut the triangle. Each side keeps its middle third, which is nine divided by three, or three centimetres.
<bookmark mark='corner'/>A cut corner has an angle of sixty degrees and two sides of three centimetres. That makes it equilateral, and each cut edge is three centimetres too.
<bookmark mark='hexagon'/>All six sides of the shape left are three centimetres. It is a regular hexagon.

<bookmark mark='corner'/>Each cut corner is a right angled triangle, with both short sides three centimetres.

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step three, find the cut edge using the theorem of Ziva. The cut edge is the long side of the right angled corner.
<bookmark mark='calc'/>Three squared is nine, and nine plus nine is eighteen. The cut edge is the square root of eighteen, about four point two four centimetres.
<bookmark mark='octagon'/>The octagon has sides of three centimetres and four point two four centimetres, in turn.
